headline: Farmers struggle as fertiliser prices soar amid artificial crisis
summary: Despite government claims of adequate stocks, farmers across 10 districts report severe shortages and inflated open-market prices.
details: Farmers across at least 10 districts are struggling to obtain fertiliser from government-designated dealers, forcing many to buy from the open market at significantly higher prices.
In some areas, 50kg sacks priced at Tk 1,050–1,350 are being sold for Tk 1,650-2,150, with some farmers reporting they cannot secure enough quantities even at these inflated rates.
Farmers allege that dealers are secretly selling fertiliser to retailers instead of farmers at government-fixed prices, creating a local monopoly and artificial shortage.
Agriculture ministry data shows stocks of 13.65 lakh tonnes against a demand of 13.21 lakh tonnes for July-September, leading officials to call the shortage a 'planned conspiracy'.
The crisis has led to unrest, including an incident in Kurigram's Bhurungamari upazila where angry farmers broke into a warehouse and took 197 sacks of urea.

Experts from the Centre for Policy Dialogue suggest that weak government oversight and the lack of an effective dealer database allow some individuals to hold multiple licences and exploit the market.
The agriculture ministry has already taken action against several dealers, including the cancellation of five dealership licences.
caption:
Fertiliser prices are skyrocketing as farmers face a severe shortage despite government claims of adequate stocks.

Farmers across at least 10 districts are struggling to obtain fertiliser from government-designated dealers, forcing many to buy from the open market at significantly higher prices.

In some areas, 50kg sacks priced at Tk 1,050–1,350 are being sold for Tk 1,650-2,150, with some farmers reporting they cannot secure enough quantities even at these inflated rates.

Farmers allege that dealers are secretly selling fertiliser to retailers instead of farmers at government-fixed prices, creating a local monopoly and artificial shortage.

Agriculture ministry data shows stocks of 13.65 lakh tonnes against a demand of 13.21 lakh tonnes for July-September, leading officials to call the shortage a 'planned conspiracy'.

The crisis has led to unrest, including an incident in Kurigram's Bhurungamari upazila where angry farmers broke into a warehouse and took 197 sacks of urea.

Experts from the Centre for Policy Dialogue suggest that weak government oversight and the lack of an effective dealer database allow some individuals to hold multiple licences and exploit the market.

The agriculture ministry has already taken action against several dealers, including the cancellation of five dealership licences.

headline: Bangladesh preparing to buy Chinese J-10CE fighter jets
summary: A draft agreement is ready as the government looks to modernize its air force with cost-effective, high-performance multi-role fighters.
details: The Bangladesh government is moving forward with plans to acquire Chinese-made J-10CE fighter jets. Advisor to the Prime Minister on Information and Broadcasting, Zahid Ur Rahman, confirmed that a draft agreement for the purchase has already been prepared.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Rahman highlighted the combat effectiveness of the J-10CE, citing its performance in simulated or real combat scenarios against advanced aircraft like the Rafale.
The advisor noted that the J-10CE is a competitive multi-role fighter capable of challenging 4.5 generation aircraft, making it a strategic choice for the nation's air defense.
Regarding the cost, Rahman stated that Chinese fighters are significantly more affordable than European variants of similar quality, such as the Rafale or Eurofighter Typhoon.
The acquisition is part of a broader effort to strengthen the air force's capabilities with modern, high-performance aircraft at a sustainable cost.
caption:
Bangladesh is eyeing a major air force upgrade. A draft agreement is ready to acquire Chinese J-10CE fighter jets.

The Bangladesh government is moving forward with plans to acquire Chinese-made J-10CE fighter jets. Advisor to the Prime Minister on Information and Broadcasting, Zahid Ur Rahman, confirmed that a draft agreement for the purchase has already been prepared.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Rahman highlighted the combat effectiveness of the J-10CE, citing its performance in simulated or real combat scenarios against advanced aircraft like the Rafale.

The advisor noted that the J-10CE is a competitive multi-role fighter capable of challenging 4.5 generation aircraft, making it a strategic choice for the nation's air defense.

Regarding the cost, Rahman stated that Chinese fighters are significantly more affordable than European variants of similar quality, such as the Rafale or Eurofighter Typhoon.

The acquisition is part of a broader effort to strengthen the air force's capabilities with modern, high-performance aircraft at a sustainable cost.
